campaigns.opening: I am writing in strong support of CMS's proposed rule on prior authorization. Every day, patients are forced to wait weeks or months for treatments their doctors have already prescribed. Prior authorization requirements delay necessary care, drive up costs, and put patients at risk. Doctors, not insurance companies, should decide what care patients need. I urge CMS to finalize and strengthen this rule by requiring 24-hour decisions, mandating clear justifications for all denials, and ensuring a robust appeals process. Patients can't afford to wait.

representatives.text: Most of our RX in Reach Coalition members, such as GASCO and organizations like the American Society of Clinical Oncology, support the goals of faster drug access, however, the technical complexity, financial strain, and administrative challenges posed by the current draft will create an unreasonable burden of time and finances on provider practices and hospitals; causing delays in the care of patients.

We encourage CMS to provide clear technical guidance on operationalizing medical-benefit drug criteria within the PA API, including how payers should represent multi -step clinical criteria (e.g., diagnosis verification, biomarker requirements, site-of-care constraints) in a structured, API-accessible format.

PA's create an administrative burden for providers and their staff to answer the multitude of clinical questions and the time it takes to submit clinical proof for what a patient needs and what providers recommend according to medical standards.

We urge CMS to encourage greater payer standardization through technical interoperability requirements and expectations. 3 This will help ensure that payers process similar requests consistently across plans and systems, creating an overall more streamlined process.

While I support the intent of this proposal, I encourage CMS to consider the implementation burden on healthcare organizations and to provide adequate support, education, and transition time for healthcare systems adopting new interoperability requirements.

We further recommend that CMS: •Finalize the proposed expedited review timelines and strengthen enforcement mechanisms for noncompliance. •Require automatic approval when payers fail to meet applicable review deadlines. •Require continuity-of-care protections that maintain access to existing therapy during pending appeals or patient transitions between health plans.

What would be the benefits and burdens of requiring certification of payer API technology for payers, providers, and patients? • If ONC were to establish criteria for payer API technology, should CMS require certification to meet payer API requirements, or should such certification be made available solely on a voluntary basis?
For insurers, not only do we recommend that the proposal to make this information sharable between payers be made available, but we urge CMS to require plans to access and honor that information.

Requiring impacted payers to expand their APIs to process drug PAs electronically will lead to less administrative burden, eliminate time- consuming faxes, phone calls, and paperwork that routinely delay dispensing needed medications, and allow pharmacists to focus on clinical care, patient care, medication safety, and help patients start prescription drug treatments without unnecessary interruption.

For CF patients, their diagnosis will never change; they will take many of the same drugs throughout their lifetime and it is unnecessary to require providers to continuously request reauthorizations and provide duplicative information in order to demonstrate the medical necessity of these therapies.

However, many payors will not allow the laboratory to initiate the prior authorization and/or require that the prior authorization be initiated prior to the date of service, which they define as the day that the sample was collected.

To support this, CMS should clarify that pharmacists must be able to participate in prior authorization workflows in both capacities, including: (1) accessing and acting on prior authorization requirements when dispensing medications; and (2) initiating, submitting, and supporting prior authorization requests when acting as the rendering provider.

Natera supports CMS's recognition that prior authorization for laboratory tests can create barriers to care and coverage, particularly when a specimen has already been collected, the laboratory is ready to perform testing, and the payer rejects or denies authorization because the request was submitted after the specimen collection date.
As a result, a n order and a specimen may arrive at the laboratory without a prior authorization request having been submitted.

Additionally, Request for Information on Prior Authorization for Clinical Laboratory Services Page 3 it is important to note that some specimens cannot be re-collected easily if the original specimen degrades while waiting for prior authorization (for example, lymph nodes or tumor samples).
The burden does not end with the initial prior authorization request or denial.

For example, MA organizations commonly require prior authorization requests for Myriad’s laboratory tests to come from the ordering provider before the specimen is collected, prohibiting Myriad from obtaining the prior authorization on our own.

The Academy recommends that CMS require payers to annually review their prior authorization process based on the above metrics and report to their provider network the complete list of items and services, including medications, that are subject to prior authorization, listing the requirements and rationale for the need for continued prior authorization based on current clinical criteria. 4.
